sub_chapter_briefs.title: The Pattern
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: Mara plays the recorded signal for Tomás. He listens once, goes very still, asks her to play it again, and on the second pass identifies the encryption structure — a pre-Cascade military burst-transmission protocol, modified but unmistakable to anyone who spent three years running signals exercises with it. He tells her what that means: not a hobbyist, not a lucky scavenger. Someone rebuilt a hardened military transmitter. He names the implication she has been avoiding: the Reclamation Authority will already be hunting it.

sub_chapter_briefs.title: What He Carries
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: A brief exhale: Tomás makes coffee from his own supplies (a courier's luxury), and while his hands are busy he tells Mara about his route — six settlements, 400 miles of terrain he knows better than anyone alive on the eastern seaboard. He does not offer to guide her. He talks about the settlements the way a man talks about people he is responsible for. Mara listens and understands that he is telling her what the signal would mean to those people — warmth, medicine, contact — before she has asked him for anything. [ESCALATING THREAD PLANTED HERE: Tomás mentions, almost in passing, that one of his route settlements — Harrow Station — was 'cleared out' two years ago by what people call a Reclamation sweep; he does not know the details, only the absence. This small fact will resurface with greater pressure in Chapter 4 when Mara and Tomás pass through Harrow Country, and will explode in Chapter 6 when Aldric Senn's identity and his role in the Harrow Station massacre is revealed — the thread starts as geography, becomes history, becomes accusation.]

sub_chapter_briefs.title: The Condition
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: Tomás agrees to guide Mara west — but only after extracting a specific promise: whatever she finds at the signal's source, whatever it is, she shares it with every settlement on his route. Not the Reclamation Authority. Not a single faction. Everyone. He names the settlements by name, slowly, like a list of the dead he is trying to keep alive. Mara makes the promise. The reader is immediately inside her qualification of it — she tells herself she means it, she tells herself she will mean it when the time comes, she tells herself the promise is conditional on the signal being what she thinks it is. She does not say any of this aloud. [ESCALATING THREAD CONTINUES: this promise — made sincerely on the surface, already being eroded underneath — is the lie that will pressure Mara in Chapter 5 when Priya asks her directly what she intends to do with the broadcast, and will reach its reckoning in Chapter 7 when Mara must choose, at the transmitter, between a targeted broadcast that serves her own need to act and the open broadcast Tomás made her promise.]

sub_chapter_briefs.connects_to_book_arc: Stage 5 — Crossing the Threshold: the promise is the door closing; Mara has committed to the journey and to a moral obligation she is already beginning to hedge; the threshold is not geographic but ethical

sub_chapter_briefs.title: West
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: They pack in near-silence, Tomás with the efficiency of a man who has done this a thousand times, Mara with the controlled deliberateness of someone who knows she is leaving and does not know if she is coming back. She locks the farmhouse. She takes her logbook. She does not take the watch she was repairing — Dani's watch, the reader understands without being told — and then goes back for it at the last moment. As they move out onto the road heading west, Tomás says, without looking at her: 'The RA will have the signal by now. We have maybe four days before they have people in the field.' Mara does not answer. The chapter ends on the road opening ahead of them and the farmhouse shrinking behind — and on Mara's private thought that she does not know yet whether the signal is hope or a trap, but that she has never been able to leave a frequency unresolved.
